title: Smile and Portrait
premise: Urban explorer Kestrel Okafor documents the abandoned village of Hollowmere, where a church bell that was melted down in 1911 rings every dusk. Their investigation uncovers a 1974 theft: the village's last surviving family took a consecrated reliquary when the parish was dissolved, and every resident since has vanished the moment they tried to sell the land. The bell is not a haunting but a summons, counting down to the signing that will erase Hollowmere's last claimant, elderly Maud Ferris, from the record entirely. Kestrel, who has survived by never believing and never belonging, must convince Maud to return the reliquary to the flooded crypt beneath the church, choosing truth and restitution over the money that would save her, and discovering that being seen by the village is the price of leaving it alive.
about_author: Theo Quintana is a former land surveyor who spent a decade mapping forgotten infrastructure across the English countryside before turning to horror. They write about places that refuse to stay on the map, and people who refuse to stay invisible.

chapters.title: Access Point
chapters.summary: Kestrel Okafor's POV. Kestrel breaks into Hollowmere's fenced perimeter to survey unmapped tunnels beneath the village, treating the place as a puzzle of drainage and subsidence, not a haunting. The beat is confident competence shadowed by the first wrong note: a church tower with no bell, yet a rope worn smooth by use.

chapters.title: The Bell That Isn't
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. At dusk, the empty tower rings. Kestrel films it, checks for speakers, finds nothing, and refuses to interpret it, logging the anomaly as 'unexplained acoustic event.' The beat is denial as armor; the reader sees the armor cracking.

chapters.title: Maud Ferris
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel finds the village's last resident, ninety-year-old Maud Ferris, living without power at the edge of the green. Maud warns her off politely, then says the bell rings 'when it wants someone.' The beat is uneasy hospitality and the first hint that Kestrel was expected.

chapters.title: Survey of Absence
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel maps tunnels that appear on no county record, finding 1974-era survey stakes and a bricked archway beneath the church. The beat is the thrill of discovery curdling as the tunnels seem laid out to funnel toward the crypt, not away from it.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Maud's POV, the novel's first shift. Maud recalls 1974: her father, the parish's dissolution, and the reliquary of Saint Aldhelm pried from the crypt altar and hidden in the family cellar. The beat is guilt as inheritance; she has kept it fifty years and never once opened the box.

chapters.title: The Papers
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A developer's agent arrives to collect Maud's signature on the final sale of Hollowmere. Maud stalls; the agent is oddly insistent, and Kestrel notices his shadow moves a half-second late. The beat is the intrusion of ordinary greed into something not ordinary at all.

chapters.title: Bell Count
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The bell begins ringing more often, and Kestrel, counting, realizes the intervals are shortening like a countdown. They cross-reference dates with parish records: every prior signing attempt coincided with a disappearance. The beat is dread through data; Kestrel's skepticism becomes a weapon that confirms the horror.

chapters.title: The Cellar Box
chapters.summary: Maud's POV. Maud finally opens the reliquary: it is empty except for a scrap of 1911 bell-metal and a name scratched inside, not her father's. The beat is the collapse of her fifty-year story; what her family took was already a replacement for something older, and older debts don't lapse.

chapters.title: Kestrel Believes Nothing
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Confronted with Maud's account, Kestrel offers rational explanations and is genuinely unable to sleep, hearing the bell through the walls of their tent. The beat is the loyal skeptic's crisis: believing would mean admitting they belong to this story.

chapters.title: The Drowned Crypt
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel dives the flooded crypt through the tunnel network and finds the original reliquary niche, scoured clean, and handprints in the silt facing outward, as if something climbed out. The beat is physical horror and awe; the tunnels were never infrastructure, they were a throat.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Left
chapters.summary: Maud's POV. Maud describes the disappearances of 1974 onward, including her sister, who 'went to the signing and never came back.' The beat is grief finally spoken; Maud has been the village's last witness, and witnesses are what it keeps.

chapters.title: The Agent Returns
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The agent returns with a second man who never blinks, pressuring Maud to sign by Friday. Kestrel photographs them and the photos develop wrong: the men are slightly transparent, and behind them the tower stands where no tower is. The beat is evidence Kestrel cannot file anywhere.

chapters.title: Loyalty
chapters.summary: Maud's POV. Maud admits she kept the reliquary not from greed but from loyalty to her dead father's last command, and that signing would free her to die. Kestrel, listening, realizes Maud is the first person who has ever needed them. The beat is loyalty as trap and as bond, both at once.

chapters.title: The 1911 Record
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. In the county archive, Kestrel finds the 1911 melting of the bell: it was sold to fund a cover-up after three children drowned in the crypt, and the bell-metal scrap in the reliquary is from that casting. The bell has been asking for its body back for over a century. The beat is justice reframed; the haunting is a claim, not a curse.

chapters.title: Return Address
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel works out the mechanics: the reliquary, the bell-metal, and a named restitution must go back into the crypt before the signing, or Hollowmere takes its payment in people. Maud refuses; returning it means admitting her father was a thief. The beat is the theme sharpened: truth costs more than survival.

chapters.title: The Village Wakes
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The empty houses light up one by one at dusk, and figures stand at windows, patient, watching Kestrel carry boxes toward the church. The bell rings continuously now. The beat is siege-like terror; the village is no longer hiding that it is populated by everyone it kept.

chapters.title: Maud's Refusal
chapters.summary: Maud's POV. Maud locks the reliquary away and prepares to sign, choosing her father's memory over the truth. The bell stops ringing for the first time in weeks, which is worse. The beat is betrayal and heartbreak; the village goes silent to let her make her mistake.

chapters.title: Signing Day
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The agent and the blinkless man arrive for the signing. Kestrel breaks into the cellar, takes the reliquary, and runs for the church as the village's figures step out of their doorways, unhurried. The beat is the point of no return; Kestrel commits theft to commit justice.

chapters.title: The Descent
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel reaches the crypt as the signing begins above; the water rises, the tunnel closes behind them, and the figures of the vanished stand on the steps, not blocking the way but watching. The beat is claustrophobic climax; Kestrel must place the reliquary and speak the name scratched inside, aloud, in the dark.

chapters.title: Restitution
chapters.summary: Maud's POV. Above, Maud tears up the papers as the bell rings one final, enormous note, and the agent and his companion come apart like smoke. She hears Kestrel's voice through the floor saying a name that is not her father's: the first stolen child's. The beat is catharsis; the debt is named, and naming is the payment.

chapters.title: What the Village Keeps
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The waters recede; the crypt door opens onto morning. The village is empty in a new way: the figures are gone, the tower is a ruin, and Maud is alive at her gate. But Kestrel's survey maps now show Hollowmere on every record, with their own name listed as its cartographer. The beat is survival with a price; being seen cannot be undone.

chapters.title: Smile and Portrait
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, closing. Kestrel and Maud bury the 1911 bell-metal in the churchyard and Kestrel publishes the true survey of Hollowmere, ending their career of invisibility. On the last page, Kestrel finds an old photograph tucked in their gear: the village, whole, everyone smiling, and Kestrel standing among them. The beat is quiet, unresolved warmth; they were never an outsider, and now they never will be.
